extracted.intended_audience: geologists, natural philosophers, and advanced students of geology/geognosy
extracted.subtask_description: Classify and interpret rocks by their modes of formation (endogenous/erupted, sedimentary, metamorphic) and by diagnostic features (texture, composition, relations of contact, veins, cooling/pressure effects). Intended to guide identification and explanation of rock origin and metamorphic processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four modes of rock formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The four modes (phases) in which rocks are formed, manifested in the stratified and unstratified portions of the earth's surface, including endogenous (erupted) rocks and sedimentary strata (with metamorphism and other modes implied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this high-level division as the organizing principle: begin by treating 'endogenous' or 'erupted rocks' (compact/unstratified) and then treat the second class (sedimentary strata). The text presents detailed subgroups under each mode (e.g., granite, porphyry, basalt under endogenous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Endogenous/erupted rock grouping (granite and syenite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Granite and syenite (of different ages) are principal products of terrestrial activity; granite often traverses syenite in veins and can act as an upheaving agent. Granite may occur in large insulated ellipsoidal masses covered by a shell cleft into blocks and may be divided into concentric layers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic features: veins traversing other rocks, concentric scaling/lamination, occurrence as insulated masses or hemispherical eminences; regional examples (Hartz, Mysore, Lower Peru, Kolivan, Las Trincheras) illustrate these characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quartzose porphyry identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Quartzose porphyry commonly occurs as veins relative to other rocks; the base is often a finely granular mixture of the same elements as the larger embedded crystals. In quartz-poor granitic porphyry the feldspathic base is granular and laminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize by textural relation between base and phenocrysts, vein relationships, and the granular/laminated base in quartz-poor varieties. (See Dufrenoy & Elie de Beaumont.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Greenstones and diorite characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Greenstones and diorite are granular mixtures of white albite and blackish-green hornblende; they form dioritic porphyry when crystals are deposited in a denser base. They may occur as strata penetrating older fissures, as veins, or as globular masses resembling basalt domes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify by mineral composition (albite + hornblende), possible passage into serpentine, presence of diallage laminae, and occurrence as intercalated beds or veins. Local mining and field observations (e.g., Nailau) provide examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of other eruptive rocks (melaphyre, basalt, trachyte, phonolite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists augitic/uralitic/oligoclastic porphyries (melaphyre), basalt (with olivine and acid-soluble constituents), phonolite (porphyritic slate), trachyte, colerite; notes lamination in some (partial or always), and internal constituents like mesotype and nepheline in basalt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish these by mineralogy (e.g., olivine, nepheline), textural lamination, and reaction to acids; use microscopic and field evidence (Girard, Gumprecht) to differentiate from look-alike masses (e.g., some nepheline-bearing rocks confused with granite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plutonic vs volcanic distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference between 'Plutonic' rocks (granite, porphyry, serpentine) and 'volcanic' rocks (trachyte, basalt, lava): volcanic masses appear as band-like streams and flows from narrow openings; Plutonic masses occur as extended insulated masses, protruded rather than flowed, probably not erupted in a state of complete fusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic criteria: morphology (streams/flows vs extended masses), presence/absence of crater structures, aperture width (narrow threads for basalts), occurrence of veins vs massive bodies. Consider mobility/viscosity and eruption aperture in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooling rate and pressure effects on texture and mineralogy
rubrics_metrics.description: The texture and chemical constitution of rocks depend on pressure and cooling time: rapid cooling yields black glass with homogeneous fracture; slow cooling yields granular crystalline structure. Carbonate of lime under great pressure retains carbonic acid and cools to granular limestone; dry crystallization gives saccharoidal marble; humid method yields calcareous spar and aragonite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experimental and comparative evidence (Sir James Hall, Gustav Rose) to infer cooling histories and pressure conditions from textures and mineral phases observed in field and thin section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of temperature and mobility (viscosity) in eruptive rock character
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of fluidity (mobility/viscosity of particles) varies from granite to basalt and across geological periods; this variation influences resulting rock forms and associated substances expelled with eruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret eruptive morphology and intrusive vs effusive behavior in terms of inferred viscosity and temperature; compare granite (less fluid/protruded masses) with basalts (more fluid/flows and narrow outlets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamorphism by contact (Plutonic action) — transformations and indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Endogenous erupted rocks produce metamorphic changes (gneiss, mica slate, granular limestone) in sedimentary strata by elevating, chemically altering, and modifying internal structure. Contact metamorphism includes hardening into schistose structure under pressure and chemical modification without simple cooling solidification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for transformations in strata near plutonic bodies: conversion of schist to mica slate or gneiss, development of feldspathic and micaceous minerals, loss or alteration of fossils. Use progressive sequences and direct chemical/thermal experiments to support inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silicification and quartz penetration indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Penetration of silica into argillaceous schist produces quartz veins and transforms schist into whetstone or silicious schist; extreme silicification produces ribbon jasper. Such silicification can be accompanied by clay, lime, potash, and iron oxides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize silicification by quartz infill, ribbon banding, and associated mineral assemblages; cite localities (Oural, Elba, Tuscany) and note potential for associated galvanic effects when carbon is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth/extent of contact metamorphism (penumbra vs complete transformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact effects vary from slight transformation (a 'penumbra' near contact, e.g., basalt veins traversing chalk at Belfast) to complete conversion of entire beds into granular limestone or other metamorphic products where the eruptive mass has stronger influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess metamorphic intensity by distance from contact, degree of mineralogical change, preservation or obliteration of fossils, and comparisons across multiple localities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of specific metamorphic products (Carrara/Parian marble, gneiss, mica slate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Granular limestones such as Carrara and Parian marbles are often sedimentary strata altered by Plutonic action; gneiss and mica slate can form through contact metamorphism of limestone, schist, and other protoliths under heat/pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use petrographic, fossil, and stratigraphic evidence to trace origin: e.g., Carrara marbles occur as altered calcareous sandstones (macigno) between gneiss-like mica and talcose schist in Apuana.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of metamorphic origin in fossils and microfauna (belemnites, infusorial deposits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence, transformation, or obliteration of fossils (e.g., belemnites found in altered schists or primitive limestones) and the role of infusorial deposits (Ehrenberg) are important in proving organic influence and in diagnosing metamorphic histories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fossil preservation state (partially preserved, obliterated, or recrystallized) and microfossil assemblages to infer degree and conditions of metamorphism and to help distinguish protoliths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association-based inference: linking eruptive rock types to metamorphic outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated associations (e.g., occurrence of melaphyre with transformation of compact limestone into crystalline masses; dolomite masses associated with massive eruptives) justify inferring causal Plutonic influence even where direct contact is not obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply inductive reasoning: when two phenomena are consistently associated over wide areas, infer a causal link while acknowledging possible missing conditions when the association is not observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vein and intrusion patterns as diagnostic of eruptive processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Eruptive rocks penetrate as ramifying veins into strata or into other endogenous masses; granite may penetrate transition slate in narrow wedge-like veins and extend for miles, while basalts tend to issue from narrow fissures and form threadlike flows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map vein geometries, ramification patterns, and relations to host strata to interpret intrusion mechanisms and relative timing (e.g., granite penetrating transition slate over miles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of dolomite via Plutonic influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Dolomite masses (e.g., Southern Tyrol) present marked metamorphism: cavities covered with rhomboidal magnesian spar crystals, absence of stratification and fossils, granular aggregation of dolomite crystals, talc laminae, and serpentine masses implying transformation related to eruptive action and vapors in fissures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose dolomitization linked to plutonic action by textural uniformity, crystalline fabric, lack of fossils, and associated mineral assemblages; consider fissure-controlled vapor pathways as mechanisms even when direct contact is not apparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental and analogical methods to infer metamorphic processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments on fusion, devitrification, cementation, and casting (and analogies with metallurgical transformations like steel formation) illuminate metamorphic processes; e.g., devitrification and cementation experiments show transition from fibrous to granular textures under heat and pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ laboratory fusion and pressure experiments, and analogies from industrial metallurgy and crystallography, to interpret field observations and to test hypotheses about temperature/pressure histories and textural evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallographic and thermal anisotropy effects on metamorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat can induce opposite actions in crystalline bodies (expansion in one axis, contraction in another), and differences in temperature modify particle arrangements during crystallization, affecting crystal form and rock texture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use crystallographic observations (dimorphism, anisotropic thermal expansion) to explain fabric development in metamorphosed rocks and to interpret directional deformation or textural anisotropies.
